items.title: China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up new hardware
items.summary: The Top 500 list records the fewest new entrants in its history amid a massive shift in compute infrastructure investments towards AI factories.
items.body: China's LineShine remains the world's highest-performing supercomputer, according to the 68 th edition of the Top500 list published at SC26 in Chicago on Monday. For the first time in decades, the supercomputer ranking saw exceptionally few additions despite unprecedented demand for high-performance computing hardware, as the vast amounts of compute resources deployed these days are destined for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers rather than traditional supercomputers. Top 10 supercomputers unchanged China's LineShine , installed at the National Supercomputer Center in Shenzhen, offers sustained FP64 compute performance of 2.198 FP64 ExaFLOPS in the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark at 42.22 MW. The machine relies on the homegrown LingKun platform with 304-core Armx9-based LX2 processors clocked at 1.55 GHz (13,789,440 cores in total) and the proprietary LingQi interconnect. Unlike the other four exascale-class supercomputers, LineShine does not use any compute accelerators and exclusively relies on CPUs, which is largely why it only gains 3.6X performance when moving from FP64 to mixed-precision data, which is lower than systems that use low-precision accelerators. …

items.summary: The Bureau of Industry and Security has announced a new interim final rule to ensure restrictions on the export of physical AI hardware cannot be bypassed by accessing it remotely in data centers around the world.
items.body: New steps have been taken to ensure that countries and companies that are not on whitelists that would allow them to import advanced AI hardware cannot use cloud-based workarounds. The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has today unveiled an interim final rule, or IFR, in collaboration with the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council, aimed at backing up existing limitations on the export of hardware built by companies like Nvidia to non-whitelisted companies based in countries such as China. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements" using data centers in third-party countries, a statement explains. items.title: Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
items.summary: The emergence of AI has seemingly posed a threat to high-precision FP64 computation, but AMD doesn't think the HPC world is moving away from those complex calculations in the wake of AI.
items.body: While AI continues to reshape industries across science and mathematics, traditional supercomputing has seemingly taken a back seat. However, AMD's Scott Tease told Tom's Hardware Premium that most HPC sites “recognize that AI will never replace HPC,” and suggests that building a heterogeneous compute stack is the best path forward to tackle bleeding-edge research, despite Nvidia pushing performance on lower-precision data types higher for AI workloads at the cost of native performance for the important double-precision FP64 format that’s critical for HPC workloads. A heterogeneous compute stack brings together quantum, HPC, and AI under one roof, a fleet that AMD is helping pilot at Oak Ridge National Laboratory alongside IBM. Tease is AMD’s corporate vice president of HPC and sovereign AI, who joined the company earlier this year after more than a decade at Lenovo (and, before that, another 13 years at IBM). We spoke with Tease ahead of SC26 to get a read on the state of HPC, how it intersects with AI, and what’s actually driving the research community in a time when computer chips are driving headlines about international espionage plots. items.title: AMD grabs over 40% of new TOP500 list for supercomputers, up 14% since last year
items.summary: AMD's Lux supercomputer debuted at position 14 on the new TOP500 list published during SC26. It's one of two machines AMD is developing as part of a $1 billion deal with the U.S. Department of Energy.
items.body: With the coming of SC26, also comes a fresh edition of the TOP500 list, which ranks the world's most powerful supercomputers. The newly released list illustrates that AMD powers 40% of the list, up 14% compared to 2025. AMD-powered systems now tally up to 202 on the list, up from 177 last year. New to the list is Lux, a “SI + HPC supercomputer” developed by AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), which debuted at position 14. AMD’s representation in the top 10 is familiar. After debuting in June, China’s LineShine remains in the top slot. El Capitan, powered by AMD chips, is in the second slot, followed by Frontier in third, HPC7 in sixth, and HPC6 in eighth, the same as the most recent TOP500 list. Lux was announced a little over a year ago in a $1 billion deal between the DOE and AMD to develop two supercomputers. This is the first of the two, and the first time it’s been on the TOP500. The system was built by HPE and developed by AMD and DOE as part of the U.S. government’s Genesis Mission. items.title: Nvidia announces Rubin HPC GPU with 'record number of CUDA cores' at Supercomputing 2026
items.summary: Nvidia took the wraps off its Rubin HPC GPU at Supercomputing 2026. This new GPU will give scientists, engineers, and analysts over 50,000 CUDA cores to speed up agentic HPC workloads when it arrives in 2028.
items.body: The Supercomputing 2026 conference is under way, and despite continuing turmoil elsewhere in the company, Nvidia has lots to reveal at the show. Foremost among its announcements today, Nvidia took the wraps off a new member of the Rubin GPU family called Rubin HPC , a chip that the company says is meant to accelerate agentic workflows and simulation for scientists, engineers, and analysts working with large data sets. To accelerate those most demanding workloads, Nvidia says Rubin HPC has the highest number of CUDA cores on any of its GPUs - "more than 50,000" - which might imply that this chip uses a configuration similar to the four-die Rubin Ultra GPU, which links those dies together using NVLink-C2C. Today's Rubin GPU has 224 SMs and 28,672 CUDA cores, so scaling compute resources to the degree Rubin HPC does would necessarily require more dies on a package. Nvidia didn't reveal more details of the chip's physical layout alongside the announcement. (The representative image shared by the company wouldn't appear to take this into account.) items.title: Intel bets on Classiq acquisition to turn Quantum efforts into commercially viable business
items.summary: Intel aims to turn its quantum computing research effort into a commercial business by combining its silicon spin-qubit technology and manufacturing capabilities with Classiq’s established software platform and customer base.
items.body: After having spent more than a decade pursuing quantum computing research, Intel is making its first real push at commercializing its efforts. First, with the pending acquisition of quantum computing company Classiq, which has an existing list of enterprise customers. Intel says it'll be the only company that can produce qubit chips and cryogenic control electronics at scale; the deal would give it a complete top-to-bottom hardware-to-software stack, and Intel will also gain the chance to become a leading vendor of quantum computing products. Intel's acquisition of Classiq is expected to complete in the first half of 2027. items.title: Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 review: A quiet and compact Wildcat
items.summary: With an Intel Wildcat Lake CPU, the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 PC runs cool and quiet, but is only suitable for casual users. Due to the prices of RAM and storage, trying to save money using entry-level silicon doesn’t work as well as it used to.
items.body: Minisforum’s Intel-based M2 line includes mini PCs with powerful processors such as the Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H (with 16C/16T CPU and B390 graphics), and the Core Ultra 7 356H (16C/16T). But there are more modest systems, too. The $450 3D bioprinter makes ELM research more accessible, as bioprinters usually cost over $100,000. Synthetic biology is like combining engineering with microbiology, treating microbes as machines and physical building blocks to achieve various functions. In the journal ACS Applied Polymer Materials, biologist Anne S. Meyer et al. published a 3 D Bioprinting of Engineered Living Materials paper in August.
